meta.subtitle: Margins, cash conversion and modest net leverage support the business; at 36.8x trailing earnings the shares sit close to fair value

advisories: model vs Street expected return diverge by 63pp — informational, not scored

analystSentiment.commentary:
GE Aerospace reported Q2'26 revenue of $13.3B, {+ +21.1% YoY +}, at an operating margin of 18.6%, the same level as its FY25 margin. Operating margin has risen in each of FY23, FY24 and FY25, free cash flow nearly doubled in FY25, and net debt is 1.0x trailing EBITDA. The operating record is not the debate; the price is.

At $312.04 the shares trade on 36.8x trailing earnings, 33.1x trailing EV/EBITDA and ~31.8x consensus FY27E EPS of $9.82. Our Base case values the shares a year out at today's trailing multiple on FY27E earnings, a few turns below today's 39.5x multiple on current-year earnings, for $361. That multiple and the even split between our Bull and Bear cases decide the label; both are judgments, argued under Valuation.

We rate the shares HOLD with a $325–$380 target range. Our weighted fair value of $340.50 sits +9.1% above the price, just short of the +10.0% a BUY needs, against a Bear-case downside of -19.2%.

executiveSummary.companyOverview:
General Electric Company, doing business as GE Aerospace, designs and produces commercial and defense aircraft engines, integrated engine components, electric power and aircraft systems. Its company description lists two segments: Commercial Engines & Services, which builds jet engines and provides maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO) services and spare parts, and Defense & Propulsion Technologies, which serves governments, militaries and commercial airframers under brands including Avio Aero, Unison, Dowty Propellers and Colibrium Additive.

The company is based in Evendale, Ohio. FY25 revenue was $45.9B and FY25 net income was $8.7B. The market capitalization is ~$323.8B at a share price of $312.04.

thesis.label: HOLD
thesis.body: GE Aerospace lifted its operating margin to 18.6% in FY25, and free cash flow rose from $3.7B in FY24 to $7.3B in FY25. **The business is executing, but the valuation already reflects much of it.** Our Base case has FY27E consensus earnings arriving and the multiple narrowing modestly as they become the current year, which leaves the shares close to fair value. We rate them HOLD with a $325–$380 target range. The upside case is that the market keeps paying today's current-year multiple as earnings step up; the downside case is that the step slips by a year.

catalysts: The next quarterly report: revenue growth near the Q2'26 pace would run ahead of the consensus FY26E path.
Revisions to FY27E consensus EPS, the earnings level our Bull and Base cases rest on.
Any change in the repurchase pace, which drives per-share earnings and the direction of net debt.
risks: Valuation: a 36.8x trailing P/E leaves little room for a growth miss.
Earnings path: consensus FY26E EPS sits below FY25, so the case leans on the FY27E step.
Balance-sheet direction: net debt has risen for two years and the trailing current ratio is below one, discussed under Financials.

income.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December.

financials.incomeCommentary:
Revenue grew from $35.3B in FY23 to $38.7B in FY24 and $45.9B in FY25, with growth of {+ +9.5% +} in FY24 and {+ +18.5% +} in FY25. Operating income rose faster, lifting the operating margin from 10.5% in FY23 to 13.8% in FY24 and 18.6% in FY25. That is operating leverage: profit grew faster than revenue in each year.

The latest quarter extends the run. Q2'26 revenue was $13.3B, up year over year at the pace noted above, and the quarter's operating margin matched the FY25 level. On a trailing-twelve-month basis the operating margin is 18.1% and the net margin is 17.7%.

Net income needs care. It exceeded operating income in each of FY23, FY24 and FY25, at $9.5B, $6.6B and $8.7B, so non-operating items lifted the bottom line in every year, by a wide margin in FY23 and a narrow one in FY25. Our data does not let us size those items, so we anchor recurring earnings to operating income rather than to net income or diluted EPS. Gross margin is not available in our data, so we cannot separate pricing from mix within the margin gains.

balance.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December.

financials.balanceCommentary:
Total debt was $20.5B in FY23, $19.3B in FY24 and $20.5B in FY25. Cash and short-term investments fell over the same years, from $15.2B to $13.6B and $12.4B. Net debt therefore rose from $5.3B in FY23 and $5.7B in FY24 to {- $8.1B -} in FY25. On a trailing basis net debt is 1.0x EBITDA, a modest load for a business with the cash generation set out below, so the level is not a concern; the two-year rise is the part that matters. Interest coverage is not available in our data, and we do not state it.

Total equity fell from $28.6B in FY23 to $19.6B in FY24 and $18.9B in FY25. Share repurchases over the same two years were $5.8B and $7.6B. In FY24, net income more than covered that year's buyback, so repurchases explain only part of the FY24 equity decline. Our data does not show the remainder, and we do not assign a cause.

Liquidity is the weak point. The current ratio slid from 1.33 in FY23 to 1.09 in FY24 and 1.04 in FY25, and it stands at {- 0.98 -} on a trailing basis, meaning current liabilities exceed current assets. We have no breakdown of current liabilities, so we cannot say what drives it. Set beside the cash balance above, we read the ratio as a thin working-capital cushion rather than a funding problem.

cashflow.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December.

financials.cashflowCommentary:
Operating cash flow rose from $4.7B in FY24 to $8.5B in FY25, while capital expenditure was $1.3B in FY25. Free cash flow reached $7.3B in FY25, against $4.3B in FY23 and $3.7B in FY24, and the FCF margin moved from 12.2% to 9.5% and then {+ 15.8% +}.

Share repurchases, set out beside equity above, are the main use of cash in our data. Dividends paid are not available in our data.

At the current price the trailing FCF yield is 2.6%. That is a thin cash return for a holder today, so the investment case depends on growth rather than on the current cash yield.

multiples.note: Peer multiples pending a peer data source.

valuation.multiplesCommentary:
On trailing numbers GE Aerospace trades at 36.8x earnings, 6.4x sales and 33.1x EV/EBITDA. We have no peer multiples on a comparable basis, so we judge the multiples against the company's own earnings path.

Three P/E figures frame the debate. The trailing earnings multiple covers the last twelve months. The vendor labels a 39.5x multiple next-twelve-months, but it matches the price over consensus FY26E EPS of $7.91, so we read it as a current-year multiple. It sits above the trailing one because FY26E consensus EPS is below FY25 diluted EPS of $8.14; that comparison sets a consensus mean against reported diluted EPS, which carries the non-operating items noted under Financials, so it may not be like for like. On FY27E consensus EPS of $9.82 the multiple falls to ~31.8x.

We value the shares a year out, when FY27E will be the current year, and compare each scenario's multiple with today's current-year multiple, the like-for-like reference.

The Street is constructive: 22 analysts split Buy 18, Hold 3, Sell 1, with a consensus target of $396.81, a median of $400.00 and a range of $347.00–$450.00. Even the lowest target sits above the price.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: FY27E consensus EPS of $9.82 is met and the market keeps paying today's 39.5x current-year multiple on it, so the full earnings step reaches the price, just below the $388.84 52-week high. For it: Q2'26 revenue growth ran well ahead of the FY26E path, and the Street targets cluster near this level. Against it: that multiple is paid on a year when consensus EPS dips, and a multiple set on a dip year may not survive the return to growth.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: The same FY27E consensus EPS is met, and a year out the market pays today's 36.8x trailing multiple on it, a few turns below the Bull case's current-year multiple. For the compression: once earnings grow again after the FY26E dip, the multiple on current-year earnings has less reason to stay above the trailing one. Against it: every Street target sits above the price and margins are still rising. Holding the Bull case's multiple would derive BUY, so this anchor decides the label.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: The FY27E earnings step slips by a year: earnings a year out stay near the $7.91 FY26E consensus, and the market pays the ~31.8x it now pays on FY27E earnings, since without the step it has no reason to pay up for a dip year. The price breaks the $268.91 52-week low. We go no lower because a deeper multiple cut would need a downturn in air travel or defense budgets, a tail we leave outside the scenarios; the past year's low shows the market has paid less recently.

valuation.scenarioCommentary:
We weight the Base case at 50% and the Bull and Bear cases at 25% each. That gives a weighted fair value of $340.50, expected upside of +9.1%, Bear-case downside of -19.2% and reward/risk of 0.47×, which derives HOLD.

The call is close, and two inputs decide it. The first is the Bull/Bear split: moving a few points of weight from Bear to Bull derives BUY. For more Bull weight, Q2'26 revenue growth ran well ahead of consensus, operating margin rose for three straight years and every Street target sits above the price. For more Bear weight, consensus FY26E EPS sits below FY25 diluted EPS, so on the consensus basis earnings have not tracked revenue, and the shares trade well below their 52-week high with no source in front of us explaining the fall. We judge the two evenly matched. The second is the Base multiple, argued in the Base driver. Both are judgments, not findings.

The label depends on the entry point. The shares slid steadily from late August to the report date, and no source in front of us explains the move. On these scenarios every close in that stretch derives HOLD except one mid-September dip below today's price, which derives BUY; a price at the $388.84 52-week high would derive SELL, and one near the $268.91 low BUY or better. Our range sits below the consensus and median Street targets; the gap is the Base multiple.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: Our financial data reports GE Aerospace as a single reportable segment, with FY25 revenue of $45.9B. The company description instead lists two segments, Commercial Engines & Services and Defense & Propulsion Technologies. The two sources disagree; we follow the company description for how the business is organized, but we have no revenue split for either segment, so we quote only the consolidated figure and no segment or regional split.

moatFactors.name: Aftermarket services
moatFactors.body: The company description pairs new engine sales with MRO services and spare parts, which ties revenue to the fleet already in service rather than to new deliveries alone. Our data does not let us attribute the FY23 to FY25 operating margin gains to services, so we rate the factor Moderate; a service revenue or margin split showing services carrying the margin would support a Strong rating.

moatFactors.name: Defense and component breadth
moatFactors.body: Serving governments and militaries alongside commercial airframers gives the company demand that does not rest on airline traffic alone. Without segment revenue, though, we cannot size the defense share, so the diversification it offers stays unmeasured.

moatFactors.name: Cash generation
moatFactors.body: The FCF margin was 15.8% in FY25, after 12.2% in FY23 and 9.5% in FY24. FY25 free cash flow covered capital expenditure but not the full repurchase program. One strong year after a weaker one does not establish that cash conversion is durable, which is why we rate this factor Moderate.

businessMoat.durability:
We rate the moat NARROW. The evidence available to us, margin expansion and free cash flow, supports a competitive advantage, but it covers a short run of years and comes without the installed-base, backlog or segment data that would show how long the advantage lasts. A WIDE rating would need that evidence.

The main threat to durability is not a named competitor but the cycle in commercial aviation and in government defense budgets. Neither is guaranteed.

points: Second-quarter pace: Q2'26 revenue of $13.3B grew {+ +21.1% YoY +}, ahead of FY25's {+ +18.5% +}. That is one quarter set against a full-year rate, not yet a trend.
Consensus expects a slowdown: FY26E revenue of ~$50.3B implies +10% growth, well below the Q2'26 pace. Our Base case accepts that path rather than betting against it.
FY27E revenue: consensus has $55.8B for FY27E, so the Street expects growth to continue beyond FY26E; the earnings step that goes with it is argued under Valuation.

Fleet in service, unconfirmed: the aftermarket tie noted under the moat could lift revenue as the fleet grows. We have no installed-base data, so this is a hypothesis we do not build into our numbers.
Per-share growth from repurchases: buybacks shrink the share count, so EPS can grow faster than net income as long as the program continues.

management.leadership: The proxy statement excerpt available to us, dated 2026-03-12, covers related-person transactions and does not name the company's directors or officers, so we do not name or assess individuals. The record shows operating margin rising in FY24 and FY25, and free cash flow conversion improving in FY25 after weakening in FY24. Without a proxy excerpt naming officers, or MD&A, we do not attribute those results to individuals.
management.capitalAllocation:
Capital allocation has leaned heavily on repurchases. FY25 repurchases of $7.6B exceeded free cash flow of $7.3B, and FY24 repurchases of $5.8B exceeded that year's $3.7B. Over those two years cash fell and net debt rose, as set out under Financials, so the balance sheet carried part of the program; we have no full sources-and-uses statement, so we do not size that share. The 0.60% dividend yield makes the dividend a small use of cash beside the buyback.

We would prefer repurchases matched to free cash flow at a 36.8x trailing P/E: a dollar spent at a premium multiple retires less earnings than at a lower one. The counterpoint is that FY25 free cash flow came close to covering the program, and the modest net leverage noted under Financials leaves room to keep it going for a while. The pace from here, rather than the past gap, is what we would judge management on.
management.governance:
Under the 2026-03-12 proxy statement, the Governance Committee reviews and approves related-person transactions above $120,000. The proxy reports none since January 1, 2025, except that Fidelity, a five percent or greater shareholder, or its affiliates served as recordkeeper or directed trustee for certain company retirement plans and received approximately $5.1 million for these services in 2025.

For a holder, this means a large shareholder also earns fees from the company. The fee is small beside the company's scale and the arrangement was disclosed, but it is a commercial tie a holder may weigh alongside Fidelity's shareholding. The excerpt is truncated and does not cover board composition, director independence or executive pay, so we make no claim about any of them.
management.insiderOwnership: The proxy statement excerpt available to us does not include director or officer ownership, so we make no claim about insider alignment.

idiosyncratic: Valuation compression: at 36.8x trailing earnings and 33.1x EV/EBITDA, a slowdown in growth or a margin stall could cut the multiple faster than earnings can grow into it. This is the core of our Bear case.
Estimate risk: our Bull and Base cases rest on consensus FY27E EPS of $9.82. A cut to that estimate would remove the earnings step the current multiple leans on.

Balance-sheet direction: net leverage is modest today, but net debt has risen for two years while repurchases ran ahead of free cash flow, and the trailing current ratio is below one. A weaker cash year with the buyback unchanged would push leverage up from a low base; the figures are set out under Financials.
risks.systemic: The cyclical exposures named under the moat, air travel for the aftermarket and government budgets for defense, are the main macro risks here. A richly valued industrial is also sensitive to interest rates and to the market's appetite for long-duration growth: a rise in discount rates can compress the multiple even if the company delivers on its estimates.

body: We rate GE Aerospace HOLD with a $325–$380 target range. Margins, FY25 cash conversion and Q2'26 growth all point the right way, and net leverage is modest. At $312.04, though, our weighted fair value sits just short of the BUY line, because we expect the multiple on earnings to narrow as FY27E becomes the current year.

What would move us to BUY: on unchanged scenarios, a price only slightly below today's derives BUY; on the fundamentals, a next quarter that keeps revenue growth near the Q2'26 pace and lifts FY27E consensus EPS above $9.82 would raise both our Bull and Base cases. What would move us to SELL: on unchanged scenarios, a rise to about our $361 Base price derives SELL; on the fundamentals, FY27E consensus EPS sliding toward the FY26E level would shift weight to our Bear case.
